Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#719. Alec Baldwin “Really, Really Didn’t Like” Documentary About Him, Filmmakers Say

'The Trial of Alec Baldwin' director Rory Kennedy and writer Mark Bailey opened up about assessing their subject's ability to be a reliable narrator in his own story and his reaction to the film during a panel at SCAD.

“The worst thing for me is to be misunderstood,” Alec Baldwin states minutes into The Trial of Alec Baldwin, the documentary about the aftermath of the death of Halyna Hutchins, who was shot and killed on the set of Rust on Oct. 21, 2021, when a prop gun held by the actor discharged live bullets into the cinematographer as well as director Joel Souza.

It’s a somewhat unsurprising confession from Baldwin, whose seemingly combative public persona has garnered as many headlines as his TV and film roles. But it’s one that reverberates throughout the film, calling into question how Baldwin’s desire to change the public’s negative perception of him — which the film argues is what ultimately put him on trial — shapes the insights he discloses on camera. Related Stories Movies Director Rory Kennedy on 'The Trial of Alec Baldwin': "If This Was Tom Hanks or Julia Roberts, I Don't Think This Would Have Gone to Trial" TV Here's What Happened Inside the Weirdly Stealth '30 Rock' Reunion

“[That question is] one that we grappled with in the film,” director Rory Kennedy said in a Q&A following a screening of The Trial of Alex Baldwin during the SCAD Savannah Film Festival on Oct. 27. “I think part of our experience was that Alec wasn’t always the most reliable narrator of himself. … So part of what we’re trying to do, because we have these questions as filmmakers — when is he acting, what is real, what is not — we want to bring the audience into those questions as well so that it’s not like we’re presenting this as here’s all the facts.

“Our feeling at the end of the day,” Kennedy continued, “is you can feel what you might about Alec — and people have, often, strong feelings one way or the other — and you may still have those feelings at the end of the film that you had going into it, but I think most people, in watching the film, will feel like there was an injustice.”

Kennedy and her husband and producing partner, Mark Bailey, began following Baldwin in March 2023, just as filming on the set of Rust was set to go back into production after Hutchins’ death, and a mere weeks before the initial charge of involuntary manslaughter brought against him was dropped. In January 2024, a grand jury re-indicted Baldwin on the same charge as the cameras continued following him.

The documentary is both biographical and culturally expository in nature, detailing Baldwin’s decades-long career onscreen and the democratic Irish Catholic upbringing that fostered the aggression often witnessed in his notable run-ins with the press. Throughout, Baldwin expresses a love-hate relationship with his profession and the microscope under which it has placed his personal life, in one scene shedding tears over his young ambitions as an actor and in another saying he’s embarrassed by his thespian pursuit.

“I find him incredibly sincere in that he believes what he’s saying when he’s saying it; he’s not trying to consciously con you,” Bailey said at SCAD. “He’s not on script when he’s saying, ‘Movies didn’t mean anything to me. I just did it for the money.’ He actually, in that moment at the kitchen table, believes that, and [his wife] Hilaria is calling him out like, ‘But honey, you don’t really think that when you go and work with students … .’

“The other piece that complicates that even further for a guy like that who doesn’t really have a filter is that he was under enormous stress and strain,” Bailey continued, referencing footage of Baldwin expressing sorrow for Hutchins’ son and reflecting on how his own children would feel if something happened to their mother. “He’s so raw because you’re catching somebody in a real moment of crisis, which was sort of, I think, courageous of him to let us in his life at that time and to let Rory be so close there. It’s kind of a remarkable thing to see somebody, in my mind, that unguarded because even if he wanted to guard himself, he is not in that place of stability to do that.”

The film ends with Baldwin ultimately being acquitted during trial proceedings yet aware that his standing in the court of public opinion will continue to require additional reframing, the work for which he says he’s willing to do. As for his own thoughts on the finished film, which premiered at Doc NYC last November and was released worldwide on Oct. 1, 2026, by Abramorama: “He really, really, really didn’t like it,” Kennedy admitted.

“It’s traumatic for him. And I think as his lawyer says at the end, he has to live with this. And despite all of his limitations, he’s a deeply caring, emotional, sensitive human, and he carries this with him,” she continued. “He had five jobs in Hollywood, all of his producing friends called him up and fired him, and he has seven kids, and then he was just annihilated in the press and in social media and people said really mean, horrible things about him and he reads them — which I would advise him not to do — but in any case, I think it’s traumatic to watch this.”

Speaking to Baldwin’s specific feedback, Kennedy added, “He didn’t particularly like our take in sort of focusing on things like the voicemail [in which he called his daughter, Ireland, a pig in 2007] and where he sort of misbehaved historically or wasn’t at his best, so I think it was complicated for him. But, over time, and now that it’s gone on the festival circuit and people have seen the film, and people who he respects have seen the film and feel like it really helps do this story justice and helps people really understand what he went through. … I think for him, and for so many people around him who care about him, they’re like, ‘This really helps you understand what happened.’ ”

#717. TV Ratings: Blue Wave Fuels Surge in Midterm Election Night Viewing, NBC Leads Primetime

If the numbers hold, NBC will be the first broadcast network to win an election night in total viewers since 2012.

A dominant showing by Democrats in the 2026 midterms also resulted in — at least for one night — a realignment in viewing of election night news coverage.

Early data from Nielsen shows NBC leading primetime Tuesday night, by a wide enough margin that it will likely hold up through further adjustments to the ratings. That’s a big change from the 2022 midterms, when NBC finished fourth among the six most watched news outlets. NBC also claimed the most watched live stream of election night with its “Kornacki Cam,” focused solely on data analyst and video board operator Steve Kornacki.

In the likely event the preliminary ratings carry through, NBC will be the first broadcast network to lead a federal election night in total viewers since the 2012 presidential election (also topped by NBC). Election coverage across outlets is already up compared to 2022, but it might not hit the historically high levels of the 2018 midterms.

NBC averaged 6.8 million viewers in primetime, based on Nielsen fast national ratings, including out of home viewing. ABC finished second with 5.12 million viewers. The three largest cable news channels — CNN (4.159 million), MS NOW (4.156 million) and Fox News (4.04 million) — are currently within 120,000 viewers of one another. CBS is further back at 2.73 million viewers.

The fast nationals don’t include Nielsen’s big data component, so the numbers are pretty likely to change some. NBC should hold onto its primetime lead, but the cable networks are so tightly bunched that the order could easily get mixed up. This story will be updated, including comparisons to networks’ performance four years ago, as more ratings data becomes available.

The combined total of 27.05 million viewers across the six networks is already ahead of the final, 12-network total for the 2022 midterms of 25.43 million. The 2018 total of 36.11 million viewers across 11 outlets, the highest for a midterm election night this century, is probably out of reach.

NBC also had a sizable lead in the core TV news ad demographic of adults 25-54, averaging 2.93 million in primetime. ABC (1.71 million) and CNN (1.55 million) followed, while Fox News (800,000), CBS (771,000) and MS NOW (764,000) were tightly bunched. Fox Business, which simulcast the Fox News feed, drew 323,000 viewers and 77,000 adults 25-54.

The live stream of the Kornacki Cam generated 29 million views across all platforms, NBC News says, including 6.1 million on YouTube. It peaked there with some 300,000 concurrent streams between 8:30 and 11:30 p.m. ET.

Nov. 4, 1 p.m. Updated with out of home ratings from Nielsen.

#716. With God on Their Side: Bob Dylan & Pope Leo XIV Commune at the Vatican

The musician is set to play a show at the Palazzo dello Sport in Rome.

This week, Bob Dylan is knock, knock, knockin’ on heaven’s door — well, arguably the closest earthly thing to it — with the folk-rock icon meeting Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican on Wednesday (Nov. 4).

The Catholic headquarters revealed that the two figures had linked up by sharing a photo on Instagram of them shaking hands. With the pope smiling warmly in his usual traditional white robes, Dylan wears a hooded black zip-up underneath a jacket and looks at the Bishop of Rome intently.

“Pope Leo XIV met with American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan in a private audience on Wednesday, November 4,” the caption simply reads.

Other snaps from the meetup show the two men in conversation while sitting together at a table and posing together in front of a piece of artwork. Another photo features them standing and talking as Dylan leans against an umbrella.

According to Vatican News, their meeting was “brief, consisting of greetings and a few lighthearted exchanges.” The pope also apparently gifted Dylan a rosary, while the musician returned the favor by giving him a copy of his Chronicles: Volume One memoir.

Pope Leo XIV ascended to the religious institution’s top job in May last year following the death of Pope Francis, becoming the first American-born cardinal to do so. He recently made headlines — and history — by voting via mail-in ballot in the United States midterm elections, which ended with Democrats reclaiming power over both the House of Representatives and Senate.

His meeting with Dylan comes one day ahead of the 10-time Grammy winner’s planned performance at the Palazzo dello Sport, the latest stop on his Rough and Rowdy Ways Tour. He’s charted 81 entries on the Billboard 200 over the course of his career, topping the tally five times.

This has been a pretty rough week for "Star Trek" royalty on this 60th anniversary year with the deaths of both Walter Koenig, "Star Trek's" Lt. Pavel Chekov on Sunday, Oct. 25 and Patrick Stewart, the storied sci-fi property's Captain Jean Luc-Picard on Wednesday, Oct. 28.

With the passing of Walter Koenig at the age of 90 this past week, franchise luminaries of all degrees are coming out with heartfelt condolences, kind words of remembrance, and tearful reflections.

William Shatner, 95, and George Takei, 89, represent the final remaining members of the U.S.S. Enterprise's core crew from "Star Trek: The Original Series" and they both took to social media to express their deep sorrow over losing one of their fellow travelers in the final frontier.

"I am deeply saddened to learn of Walter Koenig’s passing," Shatner posted on Instagram.

"Although we did not know each other well away from the set, we shared the later seasons of the original 'Star Trek' series and the six films that followed. What I observed, and what so many fans have expressed over the years, was a man who genuinely loved the 'Star Trek' community.

"At conventions, Walter was rarely content to remain behind a signing table. He preferred to be among the people who had kept 'Star Trek' alive for so many decades. That kind of genuine connection is rare, and it will be remembered by everyone who came into contact with him.

"My condolences to his family, his friends, and the countless fans whose lives he touched."

George Takei, who portrayed Lt. Hikaru Sulu and co-starred with Koenig on two seasons of "The Original Series" from 1967-69, as well as six subsequent "Star Trek" feature films, offered similar thoughts in memoriam.

"My heart is heavy. Walter Koenig, our Ensign Pavel Chekov, passed away early today," Takei shared on his Instagram page.

"Walter and I met on the bridge of the Enterprise in the 1960s, and we stayed friends for nearly six decades. When Brad and I married in 2008, Walter stood beside us as our best man. Just last month, on Sept. 14, he turned 90, on the same day Brad and I celebrated our 18th wedding anniversary. I will always treasure that he and I shared that date.

"Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too.

"Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course."

Maya Hawke has boarded director Matt Johnson’s Magic: The Gathering, the live action feature from Legendary Entertainment and based on Hasbro’s iconic trading card game.

The owner of the UFC, WWE and IMG is betting on live sports being a growth engine for years to come, with the FIFA World Cup boosting its On Location business.

TKO Group Holdings raised its guidance for the second straight quarter as the UFC and the FIFA World Cup helped propel its business in Q3.

The owner of UFC, WWE and IMG reported revenue of $1.36 billion in the quarter, up 21 percent from a year ago, with net income of $277.9 million, up from $171.1 million a year ago. Adjusted EBITDA rose by 54 percent to $555.7 million.

“Our third quarter performance reflects the secular tailwinds powering live events and experiences around the world, and TKO’s assets sit front and center of that premium ecosystem,” said Mark Shapiro, President and COO of TKO. “As we close out what we’ve called our year of execution, our decision to raise full-year guidance for the second time this year is the clearest expression of our conviction across the entire portfolio. Our business is durable and our fundamentals are solid, with the vast majority of our existing revenues locked in for the next five to seven years. Macro trends are firmly in our favor, every facet of sports consumption is pointing north, and we see substantial runway ahead.”

The company’s new guidance for full year 2026 to $5.790 billion to $5.830 billion for revenue and $2.295 billion to $2.315 billion for adjusted EBITDA.

The UFC was the biggest driver of growth, with revenue surging by 60% to $519.2 million in the quarter thanks to strong growth in media rights, sponsorships, live events and consumer products and licensing. Adjusted EBITDA rose by 72 percent to $285.3 million.

At the WWE, total revenue fell by 1 percent to $399.3 million, due to a decrease in live events and hospitality revenue, offset by increases in media rights and consumer products. Adjusted EBITDA rose 5 percent to $217.2 million.

At IMG, revenue rose 16 percent to $391.3 thanks to increases in partnerships and marketing revenue, as well as increased hospitality revenue associated with the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Adjusted EBITDA rose 89 percent to $115.9 million.

#711. The Taurid meteor shower isn't much to look at. That's why I love it

The Taurids produce only a handful of meteors an hour. That sounds disappointing, but I've learned that expecting almost nothing can make this one of the most enjoyable meteor showers of the year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I used to make a basic mistake with meteor showers — I treated the zenith hourly rate (ZHR) like a timetable. If a shower were advertised at 20 meteors per hour, I'd go outside expecting something roughly every three minutes. After 10 quiet minutes, I'd start wondering what I was doing wrong. After half an hour, I'd start to doubt the whole idea of meteor showers.

The Northern and Southern Taurids cured me of all that. Two linked meteor showers that peak around Nov. 4-5 and Nov. 11-12 this year, they each manage only about five meteors per hour under ideal conditions. In reality, you may see fewer. You may spend a long time seeing none. So what's the point?

I've come to regard their paucity of "shooting stars" as a feature, not a flaw, for the Taurids have taught me to stop counting meteors and instead just observe the sky. I go outside for Taurus, the Pleiades, Auriga, and whatever else happens to be visible. If a Taurid crosses the sky, excellent. If not, the evening hasn't failed. The reason is that they are also known for occasionally producing very bright meteors, or fireballs — although "occasionally" is important. Don't go outside expecting a procession of them.

The Taurids hit Earth's atmosphere at about 18 miles (29 kilometers) per second. That's relatively slow for a meteor shower. It's one reason Taurids can be more memorable than meteors from faster showers.

For observers across much of the Northern Hemisphere, Taurus rises in the east during the evening and becomes increasingly well placed as the night progresses. Later evening into the overnight hours is therefore the best time to watch.

I love looking at the night sky around Taurus, but you really don't need to stare at it if you're looking for Taurids. The radiant is indeed within Taurus (close to the Pleiades), but meteors can appear anywhere in the sky. Look roughly east or southeast, then watch as much sky as possible for an hour or so.

This year the moon helps out. The new moon falls on Nov. 9, leaving only a young waxing crescent around the shower's peak. It sets during the evening, giving us properly dark skies later on.

My Taurid observing strategy involves doing little direct meteor observing. I'll likely head outside once Taurus is reasonably high in the eastern sky, probably sometime in the later evening, and give myself other things to look at. The Pleiades are an obvious target — it's exciting to have this little open cluster back in the evening sky. So are the Hyades open cluster and bright orangey Aldebaran, also in Taurus. I'll probably set my smart telescope on the Pleiades and leave it alone to build up a long integration while I spend as much time as I can taking in the whole sky. Meteors are a naked-eye event and demand your attention — the second you avert your gaze from the night sky, a "shooting star" will appear. All stargazers know that!

I won't travel for hours to find perfect darkness. A darker location will reveal fainter meteors, for sure, but the Taurids' occasional bright members can be seen from less-than-perfect skies. A backyard is fine for this one — make travel plans only for August's Perseids and December's Geminids (moon phases allowing).

Nor will I keep score. Meteor rates are statistical descriptions, not promises. Five per hour does not mean one meteor every 12 minutes. You could see two close together and then nothing at all for hours. We're all so used to being told exactly what to expect, but the night sky doesn't work like that — you need to be open to whatever it throws at you (or not). Once you stop expecting the sky to do what you want, meteor showers become more enjoyable.

The moon is moving out of the early evening sky this week, which is exactly what stargazers wait for at this time of year. It reaches third quarter around Nov. 1, rising later at night and leaving the evening dark. That gives us a useful 10-night window for observing before moonlight becomes an issue.

I'm planning to use it for the Andromeda galaxy. From a genuinely dark location, M31 can be spotted with the naked eye as a faint patch. From brighter suburban skies, binoculars make life much easier. The beginner mistake is expecting anything resembling the photographs. Through binoculars, I'm looking for a subtle misty glow, not spiral arms. If you want a more impressive view, get yourself a smart telescope — they do a wonderful job on M31.

There's another practical change this weekend. Daylight saving time ends across most of the U.S. and Canada on Nov. 1. The stars haven't changed their schedule, of course, but getting outside under a dark sky after dinner — and even before — suddenly becomes much easier.

Although you don't need to stare at Taurus, the Bull, to see Taurids, it's an obvious target this week. It's climbing into the eastern sky during the evening. Bright orange star Aldebaran — a red giant 67 light-years from the solar system (and the most luminous star within 100 light-years) — marks the bull's eye. It appears to sit within a V-shape of stars that forms the bull's face. This is the Hyades, the closest open cluster of stars to the solar system at just 150 light-years.

The origin story of both Taurid meteor showers is genuinely awe-inspiring. They're associated with debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke, which orbits the sun once every 3.25 years (1,200 days) — the shortest orbital period of any known comet in the solar system, according to NASA. The second comet ever discovered, Encke, was discovered in 1786 and spans about 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) in diameter. It last reached perihelion — its closest point to the sun — on Oct. 22, 2023, and is due to do so again on Feb. 10, 2027, but Earth encounters debris associated with the comet every year.

The picture is more complicated than a single comet trail. The Southern and Northern Taurids are part of the broader Taurid Meteoroid Complex, a vast swarm of interplanetary dust, rocks, comets and asteroids thought to be related to Encke. It's thought that it originates from a much larger object that fragmented as it got close to the sun, perhaps just 5,000 to 6,000 years ago or as much as 20,000 years ago. Fears that huge, mile-wide "planet killer" asteroids may still reside in the Taurid Meteoroid Complex appear to have been ruled out. Phew.

Each fall, Earth passes through different parts of this sprawling stream, producing two overlapping meteor showers — and, occasionally, the larger fragments responsible for the Taurids' famous fireballs.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#710. SM Entertainment Reports Revenue Decline On Lower Music Sales, Concert Revenue

The K-pop label said it had fewer major releases in the quarter "as our major artists focused on expanding their overseas activities."

By Elizabeth Dilts Marshall

SM Entertainment’s stock sank more than 7% on Wednesday (Nov. 4) after the label home of K-pop stars aespa and NCT reported an unprofitable quarter. The company said lower physical and digital music sales and concert revenue resulted in a 9% decline in overall revenue.

SME said it generated 291.1 billion Korean won ($205.2 million) in revenue and operating profit of 35.5 billion Korean won ($25 million), which is down 26% from the year-ago quarter. The company operated at a net loss of 1.1 billion Korean won ($775,000) for the quarter, down from a 44.7 billion Korean won ($31.5 million) profit a year ago, “primarily due to foreign exchange-related losses resulting from the appreciation of the Korean won,” Jeongmin Jang, CIO of SM Entertainment, said on a conference call discussing the quarter.

“New album sales volume decreased by approximately 70% year over year as our major artists focused on expanding their overseas activities,” Jang said.

Sales of physical and digital music fell by 51% to 47.1 billion KRW ($33.21 million). SM said it sold 1.67 million copies of artists’ releases in the quarter, driven primarily by sales of NCT 127’s album BLINGY.

There were bright spots in SM’s earnings. The company’s share of major artists’ album releases andglobal concert activities, as well as the impact of IP licensing collaborations — what the company refers to as MD/licensing revenue — increased 23.5% year over year to 62.1 billion Korean won ($43.78 million).

Additionally, revenue earned from artists’ appearances, driven by artists’ participation ininternational award ceremonies, music festivals, apparel and cosmetics advertising, and other areas increased by 21.3% to 29.2 billion Korean won ($20.6 million).

#709. AMC Theatres Rides Box Office Rebound to Record Revenue in Third Quarter

In a key box office recovery test, the mega-exhibitor saw theater visits, ticket and concession sales rise with Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' and 'Spider Man: Brand New Day' on its screens.

AMC Entertainment on Wednesday posted sharply higher box office and revenue for its third quarter as it had Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day in its theaters.

The box office momentum will help the mega-exhibitor answer to investors whether it can leverage a steadier supply of Hollywood tentpole releases, premium screen demand and film lovers returning to the multiplex to get out from under costly debt obligations.

Overall revenue was up 31 percent to $1.71 billion, compared to $1.3 billion in the same period of 2025. That compares with the most recent second quarter when AMC saw overall revenue jump 14 percent to $1.59 billion.

AMC swung to a Q3 net income of $109.3 million, against a year-earlier net loss of $298.2 million, due mainly to non-cash charges associated with a July 2025 refinancing to fully redeem 2026 debt maturities.

The adjusted EBITDA came to $347.5 million, compared to $122.5 million and representing another quarterly record. Besides being lifted by an ongoing Hollywood box office rebound, AMC is riding a premium screen gold rush at the local multiplex by offering varied immersive auditoriums like Imax, Dolby Cinema, iSense, XL and laser projection-equipped screens.

During the latest quarter, the exhibition giant saw total admissions revenue rise to $953.5 million, compared to a year-earlier $715.1 million. Food and beverage concession revenues came to $589.5 million, up from year-earlier $451.8 million.

U.S. market attendance amounted to 52 million patrons, while international markets attendance added another 22.7 million cinema-goers at overseas venues during the third quarter. That all comes ahead of a key upcoming holiday season test for AMC as The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three will play on its screens.

The latest financial results follow ongoing efforts by AMC with lenders to secure flexibility to refinance its high debt load and reduce its overall interest expense. The company recently completed refinancings to push around $4 billion in debt maturities to 2031 and 2033.

Debt refinancing deals for AMC Theatres aim to give the movie theater chain breathing room on its balance sheet to pay down its long-term borrowings and ease balance sheet strains. To exchange new debt for existing borrowings, AMC typically has had to put up as collateral theaters and related intellectual property.

“After six long years navigating AMC through unchartered waters, we can finally say with relief that we have brought our ship into port,” AMC Theatres CEO Adam Aron told analysts during an after-market call. “What you are seeing now is a company proving quarter after quarter what it can achieve when an inspired movie slate combines with a powerful fleet of movie theaters.”

Earlier, in a statement that accompanied his latest quarterly results, Aron explained that financial performance was “thanks to our industry-leading loyalty programs along with the vast and growing number of AMC’s premium large format and extra large format auditoriums, combined with disciplined cost management, superb execution and the operating leverage inherent in our business.

The CEO added, “Our success was driven by a resurgent box office, market share gains in both domestic and international markets, and the achievement of all-time record revenue per patron.”

On the analyst call, Aron commented on Paramount Skydance completing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, and touted the enlarged studio’s pledge to produce more movies with extended theatrical releases. “We’re confident that Skydance will do everything in its power to create and deliver appealing movies under both the Warner and Paramount brands going forward,” he argued.

Aron also reiterated AMC will release on its Imax screens the upcoming sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, the Brad Pitt-starrer The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Cinemark and Regal among major chains have decided against doing their own sequel releases due to Netflix’s ultra-short two-week release window on offer.

Cliff Booth will debut in theaters on Nov. 25, then hit Netflix on Dec. 23. AMC in 2027 will have two other Netflix movies on its release slate, Narnia and Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, both of which will have “a full theatrical window,” Aron said.

He also discussed AMC using AI tools in Europe to program which movies go into which auditoriums in its theaters. “The financial implications of this, if it works, could be so significant,” he told analysts about the potential labor savings and efficiencies in better targeting cinemas with the right titles.

#708. Warner Records Nashville Lays Off Five, Including EVP of Marketing Victoria Mason

Others affected include senior vp of publicity Fount Lynch and vp of radio Anna Cage.

Warner Records Nashville laid off five staff members on Tuesday (Nov. 3), Billboard has confirmed, including executive vp of marketing Victoria “Torie” Mason and senior vp of publicity Fount Lynch.

Mason joined Warner out of Nashville in 2011, starting as director of research & analytics before moving up the ranks. Lynch joined Warner Nashville in 2022, having previously served in roles at Red Light, Sony Music and Universal Music Group.

Other affected staffers include vp of radio Anna Cage, West Coast manager of Warner Artist Relations Jenna Johnson and regional manager of radio Kayla Burnett.

It’s unclear whether the layoffs are related to the $300 million in annual cost cuts announced by Warner Music Group (WMG) CEO Robert Kyncl last year. In a company-wide memo released in July 2025, Kyncl wrote that layoffs would account for $170 million of the planned cuts. “Many changes will be implemented in the next three months, with the remainder in fiscal 2026,” he wrote at the time. He characterized the reductions as “the remaining steps in our plan to help future-proof the company and unlock the next era of growth,” adding that the money saved would be reinvested in A&R and M&A.

WMG has instituted several rounds of layoffs since Kyncl assumed the role of CEO at the top of 2023, including a 4% staff cut that March, a 10% cut in 2024 and a restructuring at Atlantic Music Group (AMG) later that year, followed by cuts in AMG’s promotion department in August 2025. In July 2025, Warner Music Nashville, which reports through Warner Records, let go of four staffers amid a realignment of Warner Records’ marketing and commerce teams.

A representative for Warner Records Nashville did not respond to Billboard‘s request for comment by press time.

Aside from helping lay the foundations for modern rocketry, Jack Parsons performed a bizarre series of ceremonies to try and conjure powerful supernatural entities.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the winter of 1946, two men from very different walks of life walked into California's Mojave Desert together, where one of them became convinced an extraordinary experiment they had been conducting had finally succeeded.

One of the men was pioneering rocket scientist Jack Parsons, a self-taught chemist who helped establish what would become NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and whose innovations in rocket propulsion would help lay the groundwork for the Space Race that would erupt in the years that followed. His unlikely companion was none other than L. Ron Hubbard, then a science fiction writer who had yet to compose the writings that would form the underpinnings of the Church of Scientology that he later established.

Despite Parsons' work with rockets and his companion Hubbard's fictional writings about them, their work together in the early months of 1946 had nothing to do with rocket propulsion, spacecraft, or other technological innovations that would eventually carry humans to space. Instead, Parsons and Hubbard were engaged in an elaborate series of occult ceremonies at the time, whereby they intended to summon an elemental feminine goddess known as "Babalon" (not to be confused with Babylon) to help them bring an otherworldly entity into physical existence.

Their efforts, known today as the "Babalon Working," represent one of the most unusual affairs in American history, with tangential connections to the history of space exploration.

Given its strangeness, the episode has garnered attention from several scholars and historians over the decades, who have sought to understand a series of events at the intersection of science and the occult involving one of the most unconventional innovators behind modern rocket propulsion.

Parsons, born in 1914, would become a key figure in the early development of American rocket technologies by the 1930s and 1940s in California, ultimately helping establish what would become the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). His contributions included the historic experiments at Pasadena's Arroyo Seco on Halloween Day in 1936, which NASA now recognizes as the foundational experiments that launched JPL.

Very much in contrast with his scientific aptitudes, Parsons also cultivated an interest in ceremonial magic during this period. By the early 1940s, he had immersed himself within the California chapter of the Ordo Templi Orientis (OTO), the organization associated with the infamous British occultist Aleister Crowley and his religious philosophy known as Thelema. In 1943, Parsons became the new leader of the organization's Agape Lodge, which subsequently began operating out of his Pasadena residence on South Orange Grove Avenue.

Parsons' occult interests became particularly focused on the evocation of supernatural entities during this period, which the young rocket scientist seemed to genuinely believe could be manifested in the physical world through ritual practices. Ultimately, this led him to undertake an ambitious — and utterly bizarre — series of ceremonies aimed at conjuring what was supposedly one of Thelema's most powerful supernatural entities.

Parsons first became acquainted with L. Ron Hubbard in the summer of 1945, and shortly after meeting, Hubbard became a resident of the scientist's Pasadena home.

While Hubbard had no formal training in the occult arts, Parsons felt he demonstrated the kinds of aptitudes that would make him a promising partner for a serious ceremonial magic undertaking. Thus, in the first days of January 1946, the pair embarked on a series of rituals, which Parsons documented in a manuscript that later became known as The Book of Babalon.

"In the introduction to this text [Parsons] explained that the underlying philosophy for the Babalon Working is that the present age is under the influence of a violent force," noted University of Gothenburg scholar Henrik Bogdan in a 2016 article published in the journal Numen. "The invocation of Babalon was thus, according to Parsons, an attempt to prevent the world from being destroyed."

Specifically, Parsons believed the force of Babalon could be manifested in a specific woman. "In this sense, the Babalon Working was not only an exercise in ritual magic, but a deliberate attempt to bring a divine feminine force into human form," Bogdan notes. With this goal in mind, during the first two weeks of January 1946, the pair worked to invoke this divine feminine figure, associated with liberation and spiritual transformation according to Crowley's Thelemic system.

On January 18, 1946, Parsons and Hubbard traveled into the Mojave Desert, where, according to Parsons' later writings, a change in atmosphere involving their ritual work suddenly became apparent. Now believing their operation had been a success, Parsons declared their work completed, and the two returned to Pasadena.

Soon afterward, Parsons reported to Hubbard that his elemental mistress had seemingly manifested with the sudden appearance at his home of a blue-eyed, red-haired artist named Marjorie Elizabeth Cameron. A former member of the U.S. Navy's WAVES program, Cameron had been invited to Parsons' residence by a colleague who, like Hubbard, was also lodging there at the time. Upon seeing her, Parsons became convinced this was the elemental lover he and Hubbard had worked to conjure, thereby confirming that the Babalon Working had produced its intended result.

Soon, Parsons and Cameron began a relationship, and borrowing ideas from Crowley's 1929 novel Moonchild, Parsons now believed that his romance with Cameron could facilitate the incarnation of a supernatural force through the literal conception of a child using ritual sex magic. The result, Parsons believed, could help to bring about a transformative new dawn in humanity's spiritual development.

This phase of the Babalon Working mainly involved magic rituals and Enochian incantations performed by Parsons and Cameron, with Hubbard present and assisting (in addition to having proposed Rachmaninoff's "Isle of the Dead" as an eerie sonic backdrop for the occasion). For Parsons, the ultimate goal had been to conceive a "magical child" that would become the newborn Thelemic messiah.

Following completion of the rituals in late February 1946, Cameron left on a trip to New York, and Parsons returned to the Mojave Desert where he completed a short treatise entitled Liber 49, believing it to be a "channeled" fourth and final portion of The Book of the Law, Crowley's foundational Thelemic text.

Upon returning from New York, Cameron even claimed to have observed an unusual aerial object—something akin to what later became known as "flying saucers" in the summer of the following year—which she believed to represent the "war engine" referenced in Crowley's work.

Crowley, however, was considerably less enthusiastic about all this. Upon learning what Parsons, Hubbard, and Cameron had been involved with, the famed British occultist confided to a colleague in an April 1946 correspondence that "Apparently he [Parsons] or Ron or somebody is producing a Moonchild. I get fairly frantic when I contemplate the idiocy of these louts."

Ultimately, a growing divide between Crowley and Parsons would cost the rocket scientist his leadership of the Agape Lodge, prompting his departure from Crowley's OTO before the end of 1946. His relationship with Hubbard similarly dissolved due to Parsons' worsening financial situation. Nevertheless, Parsons soldiered on, marrying Cameron in October 1946 and continuing his efforts to usher in a new spiritual age.

On June 17, 1952, Parsons' unusual life ended prematurely when an explosion occurred in his home laboratory, resulting in fatal injuries. He was only 37 years old. Questions still surround the circumstances of his death; while it was ruled an accident, there have been allegations that it was suicide or even a murder.

During his short life, Parsons still managed to make significant contributions to the science of rocket propulsion, securing a place in the history of American space exploration — albeit one that is often overshadowed by the interest historians and scholars have taken in his occult activities.

Nonetheless, Parsons remains a key figure responsible for helping lay the early foundations for what would become America's space program. Although decades before NASA would begin sending its spacecraft in pursuit of answers to cosmic mysteries, one of its early technological pioneers had been seeking answers to such cosmic questions in a very different way: by exploring the boundary between our physical world and the supernatural realms beyond.

Anthony Testa, The Key of the Abyss: Jack Parsons, the Babalon Working and the Black Pilgrimage Decoded (2006), p. 128.

#705. Carbon radical generation by irreversible metal-to-ligand charge transfer

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) is a fundamental photoinduced process that underpins a broad range of energy- or electron-transfer events1,2. In the absence of productive substrate engagement, the MLCT excited state typically relaxes to the ground state via photophysical deactivation, reflecting its largely reversible character3,4. Here we report a class of isolable copper–heteroaryl sulfone complexes that, upon visible light irradiation, undergo an irreversible MLCT-driven fragmentation through C–S bond cleavage within the coordinated sulfone ligand, generating carbon-centered radicals. Spectroscopic and computational studies support the formation of MLCT-derived excited states and a low-barrier pathway for C–S bond cleavage. This reactivity is largely independent of the reduction potentials of the corresponding free sulfones, enabling the generation of fluoroalkyl and non-fluorinated tertiary, secondary, and primary (even methyl) alkyl radicals. We demonstrate the utility of this platform in copper-catalyzed C–H fluoroalkylation of arenes and terminal alkynes. Leveraging these MLCT-generated trifluoromethyl radicals to initiate halogen-atom transfer (XAT) from perfluorocyclobutyl iodide (I-FCB), we also achieve radical perfluorocyclobutylation–iodination of alkenes, addressing a longstanding challenge in the incorporation of perfluorocyclobutyl motifs.

#704. Watch Druski Get Down to This Viral Latin Hit With Marcello Hernandez Ahead of ‘SNL’ Hosting Debut

The boundary-pushing comedian also suggested that this will be the "last-ever" episode of the series.

Druski is dancing his way to hosting Saturday Night Live this weekend.

In a promo video posted Wednesday (Nov. 4), the content creator appears alongside SNL cast member Marcello Hernandez, and the pair momentarily get down to “Dame Hombro,” the viral Bulin 47 and Kevin Wai hit that recently hit No. 11 on the Billboard Hot Latin Songs chart. In response to Hernandez speaking Spanish at the beginning of the clip, Druski jokes, “You know I’m a little Latino too.”

That’s when the pair start singing the track’s ultra catchy hook, with Druski impressing Hernandez with his Spanish-speaking skills. Of course, the influencer isn’t actually Latino, though he has expressed his love for Latin culture and joked that he’s an “honorary” member of the community.

Released at the beginning of October, “Dame Hombro” has already been used more than 2 million times on TikTok.

Also in the promo — which comes just a few days ahead of Druski’s hosting debut on Saturday (Nov. 7) — he remarks that he’ll be leading the “last-ever episode” of SNL, to Hernandez’s confusion. That’s when Druski whispers something to him about his plans to possibly wear and say something offensive — but fans will have to wait and see what the famously line-toeing comedian actually does on the show.

The former Billboard cover star’s upcoming 30 Rock stint follows the most recent episode, which was hosted by Inde Navarette with Gracie Abrams as musical guest. As previously announced, Druski will be joined by musical guest The Strokes, after which John Mulaney and Phoebe Bridgers will share the bill the following week.

Watch Druski’s SNL promo video with Hernandez above.

#703. Coach’s Loved Leather Finish Gives Cult-Classic Handbags the Heritage Treatment

The new vintage-inspired technique makes each piece one of one.

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, The Hollywood Reporter may receive an affiliate commission.

Coach’s most-loved designs are getting an extra dose of affection with the introduction of a specialized leather finish, aptly titled Loved Leather.

To achieve this, Coach uses an innovative new treatment on either smooth or Glovetanned leather to reveal its true base color for an authentic, vintage-inspired finish. The result is the label’s best-selling styles — like the Brooklyn Shoulder Bag, the Empire Carryall and even the Margot Sandal and Margot Slingback kitten heel — with a subtly distressed look that feels entirely genuine. Related Stories Lifestyle Marilyn Monroe, Audrey Hepburn, PÖFF Garments Bring the Glitz to New Fashion Museum Near Tallinn Lifestyle Inde Navarrette, Michael B. Jordan and Yerin Ha Front David Yurman's New York-Set Holiday Campaign

Coach’s Empire Carryall collection spans from the most petite Empire 21 ($325) to the largest Empire 48 ($950+).

Smaller Brooklyn 28 also available ($350).

Equally into the Loved Leather Margot Sandal ($195), featuring an oversized buckle detail.

Thanks to their love-worn nature, each piece is completely unique. And its intentional lived-in look means you don’t have to be too precious in your day to day. As time goes on, the patina continues to develop and natural signs of wear take hold, meaning Loved Leather products only get more distinctive and special with age.

While Coach introduced Loved Leather across nearly all its categories — purses, footwear, outerwear, travel bags and small leather goods — the brand’s cult-favorite handbags are inevitably the star of the show. This includes the beloved Coach Brooklyn Shoulder Bag, the petite Teri Shoulder Bag, the oversized Soft Empire Carryall Bag 48, the east-west Empire Carryall Bag 34, the newer Kisslock Frame Bag 27 and, a versatile favorite, the Emily Shoulder Bag.

Adjustable strap extends from handbag, to shoulder to crossbody length.

Finished with two detachable straps to carry by hand or wear crossbody.

As for current accessories trends, the loved-leather look perfectly ties in to the slouchy shoulder bag moment we’re seeing this fall into winter, as structured silhouettes and hardware-heavy handbags are making way for their laid-back counterparts. These relaxed styles go hand in hand with the lived-in leather treatment seen across Coach’s messenger bags, totes and carryalls.

Also available in honey brown and chestnut brown Loved Leather, plus teak Loved Suede ($1,200).

And Loved Leather is not a one-color-fits-all situation — It comes in shades of brown, tan, black, olive and white, with both silver and brass hardware. There are even Loved Suede and Loved Denim options, two fresh takes on Coach’s signature treatment.

#702. DNC Vice Chair: “We Had to Hit the Bottom”

A leader of the Democratic blue-nami on viral videos, the billionaire tax and how everything had to go wrong before it could go right.

The Democrats and their many supporters in Hollywood had a historic election Tuesday night, and it’s leaving some of the people who orchestrated it both celebratory and trying to learn from the results.Jane Kleeb is one such person. A vice chair of the Democratic National Committee under Ken Martin who also heads up the Association of State Democratic Committees (which basically represents the Democratic party in each state and territory), she helped lead the movement that resulted in Tuesday’s many wins.

A native Nebraskan and longtime activist, Kleeb was in a giddy mood Wednesday, and also a pragmatic one. We got on the phone with her to break everything down.First I have to ask, how much of a surprise were some of these races? A few felt on the bubble coming in but others were just shockers. Does it feel that way to you?I definitely thought we were going to win the House and the Senate back because I knew the quality of candidates and the infrastructure we were building, and I thought we would win some governors’ races and break some supermajorities at the state legislative level as well. But I didn’t know it would be to this extent — that the margins would be so wide. In some of these races it wasn’t one or two percentage points; it was five or six or more. So it was a resounding victory, not just voting against Trump.So you don’t see a lot of these as “anti” votes.When I was watching some pundits [on cable news] last night people were pontificating saying this was just a rebuke to Trump. And no question it was. But it was also because Democratic organizers everywhere and candidates who looked and sounded like their communities and were also fighters. So it was all of those factors.Of course, you’ve tried to do that before. What changed?I think it’s because our candidates this cycle thought they had nothing to lose. That Donald Trump was such a threat to democracy that they were putting everything on the field and because of that it happened all across the country not just in targeted battleground states.You say nothing to lose. In your mind did you need to hit rock bottom — did 2024’s calamity enable this?There’s no question we had a major reality-check as a party in 2024. And even in 2016. We felt like we recovered some footing in 2020 but not enough to carry us. We saw that with the divisions over keeping Biden as the nominee or switching candidates 100 days out in [2024]. And that’s a picture of where we were as a party, that we couldn’t find our voice, we couldn’t find our footing. We couldn’t figure out how to communicate to the American people all of the good things we were doing. So we hit the bottom. We had to hit the bottom. When Trump won again we saw with so many of the communities that we frankly took for granted — Black voters and young voters and Latino voters — they saw Trump as a change agent and someone who would break up the status quo. And obviously he didn’t deliver on any of that, so we picked back up and said “actually we’re the party fighting for change to level the playing field.” And voters received that message.That certainly happened across the Midwest and the South. But a lot of our readers are in California, where that didn’t happen — it looks like the billionaire’s tax is going to fail pretty badly. Why couldn’t you make that case to Californians?If the tax fails it could be for a lot of reasons. Maybe it’s that people don’t like taxes, it could be that.Honestly the way it was laid out on the ballot was also confusing — you basically had a billionaire tax and a ban on a billionaire tax right next to each other, both just looking like a property tax.I think it could also have been that. I definitely still believe people are deeply frustrated by the billionaire class and want to see accountability from billionaires. So maybe it’s not a tax but maybe it’s stopping giveaways at the federal level. There are other ways to get that accountability.One thing that struck me about the election is that unlike in past party sweeps — say, the Democrats in 2008 with Obama — there was no central charismatic figure around which all these House and Senate and local races coalesced. That you did it bottom-up instead of top-down.

The difference this time was definitely the story of a team instead of a lead actor. And I think that’s where the party shines. When rely on one person to carry us through we’re going to lose that battle. That happened with President Obama during his terms. We lost 1,500 seats at the local level over his eight years because we weren’t investing in state and local infrastructure; we got so wrapped up in “Obama.” So I think we learned the hard lesson that it’s this infrastructure model that works. And we saw that this time.What would you say was the biggest surprise last night?Symone Sanders, who is from [here in] Nebraska had been talking about Mississippi. So I went down and visited. I thought ’this was a state where it could happen, but not this cycle.’ But that was a mistake. We had Brandon Presley, [a moderate Democrat] who almost won [for governor in 2023]. But we didn’t give the resources to get over the finish line. And to see what Scott [Colom] has done without those resources — if this happens [Colom is currently leading his opponent Cindy Hyde-Smith by a few dozen votes with 44,000 ballots outstanding] it’s from the sheer grit of Scott and the Democratic Party there and the candidates down-ballot.And the viral videos were insane — he did that whole pick “another protein/pick another Senator” bit to troll Hyde-Smith’s line from a debate. I don’t think I can remember a political ad as subtly effective and smile-inducing as that.He’s been great. And it does make me feel like, damn, we should have known.You do have limited resources, though, and I wonder how you spread that out now that so many states seem to be in play, places like Kansas and Nebraska and Texas and South Carolina and maybe even Alaska. It seemed a lot easier when certain red states were just automatically out of bounds. Does this indeed make where to spend your money more complicated?What is very clear from the amount of money raised this cycle is that we don’t have limited resources. There’s plenty of money in the political system. What you will hear from me and Chair Martin and many who live and work in our 57 states and territories is we can and should have permanent infrastructure everywhere, no exceptions, year-round.You don’t think there are simply some states too far gone to justify Democrats spending money in — that if, say, Florida couldn’t elect a Democratic Senator or governor in this climate, maybe it’s beyond hope for the party?

I think this is absolutely the wrong way to look at it. Colorado was red not that long ago, and then we began organizing and getting young people to vote. Georgia was red not that long ago and now look at it. [SZ: Both those states saw large influxes of Democrats from other states that Florida has not seen.] I grew up in Florida and it was a swing state. We’re starting to organize there. You have places like Colorado and Mississippi where there are cities that are blue and then you spread out to the suburbs and beyond making inroads there. Florida has that too. I think you’ll begin to see things shift significantly in places like Florida and Nebraska [where the party came close to defeating a Republican this cycle with an independent Senate candidate] as we head into 2028.Speaking of looking ahead, now the Democrats have to govern. And they have to govern with moderates and progressives and far-left activists in the came caucus. We see here in Hollywood the rifts that can happen even among Democrats — we see it, and I’m kidding but not kidding, all too well unfortunately. How do you ensure those rifts don’t happen in the next two years?I think having progressives and moderates gives us an advantage because we’ll have durable long-lasting policies that all kinds of Americans will embrace. Because the American people have all those different views too. People look at these disparities as a risk, but I see them as an advantage.

#701. 5 horror franchises that went to space... and one that absolutely should have but didn't

In space, no one can hear you scream... or laugh.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In space, no one can hear you scream... not unlike in the empty theater screens that aging horror franchises play to when the lustre has gone and their final installments limp to the public. It is perhaps little wonder that some horror franchises go to space to die... or take long breaks, at least. In celebration of Halloween, we're running down some horror franchises that made the journey to the final frontier, resulting in films that range from the sublime and outrageously campy fun to just pure awful.

Absent from the list are space horror movies that have space baked into their natural fabric. So no Event Horizon, no Alien, and no Critters 4 (they were aliens, so they just went back to space; that doesn't count).

2001 was a really weird time for the Friday the 13th franchise. New Line had acquired the series in the wake of the terrible box office returns and critical panning of Friday the 13th Part VIII: Jason Takes Manhattan. Known as "the house that Freddy built," New Line's plan was clear: pit Voorhees vs. Kruger in a battle of horror icons for the ages.

However, the studio had to keep Jason in the public eye to ensure the eventual crossover lived up to expectations. The first move in that effort, 1993's Jason Goes to Hell: The Final Friday, was an odd start. The movie apparently kills Voorhees, with his iconic hockey mask seized by the equally iconic bladed glove of Freddy Krueger at the end of the film and dragged into the dirt.

Fun bit of trivia: the hand wearing the glove isn't that of Freddy actor Robert Englund but belongs to Kane Hodder, arguably the best Jason Voorhees, meaning Hodder played both Jason and Freddy!

Still, the crossover has stalled in the preproduction process by 2001, as a script couldn't be agreed upon. New Line wanted a new Friday film but in a different environment than the typical Crystal Lake setting. After rejecting a winter-themed movie that would see Voorhees killing cross-country skiers in a snow-covered Camp Crystal Lake, New Line decided to put Jason on ice in a different way, cryogenically freezing Pamela Voorhees' baby boy and sending him to space in Jason X, the tenth movie in the series.

Jason X would see the Crystal Lake Killer slaughter David Croenberg, get his ass kicked by a feisty robot, and double up on his iconic sleeping bag kill from Friday the 13th Part VII: The New Blood (one of my favorites, massively underrated), all on the way to getting a major upgrade from some very unhelpful nanobots to become Uber Jason. Jason X has a mixed reputation and isn't regarded as one of the better entries in the series, but the movie has a load of positives going for it.

The kills are super inventive, the nitrogen head smash being arguably one of the best in a series known for over-the-top brutality; Kane Hodder is great during his final shift as Jason, and there are a load of laughs. Jason X isn't as tongue-in-cheek as one of the following movies on this list, but it is definitely self-aware and so much better for it.

In honor of arguably the best of these space-relocated horror movies, we'll rate this and the following movies in Uber Jasons out of five. For campy space-based horror featuring a character that is a fish out of water, Jason X is near perfect.

4.8 Uber Jasons out of 5. Hail to the king, baby.

Alien is often referred to as "a haunted house movie in space." The elements are all there: isolation, a hidden, poorly understood danger lurking in the shadows, victims picked off one by one. Of course, that is figurative, but Amityville in Space shows why filmmakers should never make things too literal. Amityville in Space is bad. Not so bad that it is good. So bad, it is bad.

Your opinion on Amityville as a franchise likely depends on your tolerance for utter hogwash. The first movie, The Amityville Horror, released in 1979, is an effective, often quite creepy horror. Since then, the loose Amityville Horror franchise spans nine core Amityville movies and between 50 and 90 low-budget independent additions to the franchise.

Amityville in Space is definitely at the cheapest end of the low-budget spectrum, and as the name suggests, it takes 112 Ocean Avenue further than ever before, to the year 3015 and the edge of a distant black hole.

Literally, the only thing worth watching in Amityville in Space is the hilarious opening that sees a failed exorcism attempt cause the Amityville house to literally blast off the surface of Earth like a rocket.d

Unfortunately, Amityville in Space isn't a corny "so-bad it's good" movie. It's just frustratingly bad. Perhaps disappearing into a black hole is the fate Amityville deserved all along, though with the name being in the public domain, Amityville movies will just keep coming. At least I didn't have to watch Amityville Death Toilet (yes, that really exists).

0 Uber Jasons out of 5. Avoid like a demonic pig called Jodie

Leprechaun 4 sees the franchise that launched the career of Jennifer Aniston blast its titular antagonist into space. The Leprechaun, played by the unparalleled Warwick Davis, makes the voyage to the final frontier with tongue planted firmly in cheek, and the results are bloody glorious.

The film sees the Leprechaun's attempts to woo a space princess rudely interrupted by space marines and the minor inconvenience of being blown apart by a grenade.

The Leprechaun then exacts his revenge on the spacecraft of the marines, an impressively realized set for a straight-to-video horror movie in the mid-90s.

If you want some camp horror fun on Halloween, the sight of the Leprechaun emerging fully formed from the pants of a space marine is probably going to be unbeatable.

Fans of British sitcoms will be equally delighted by the appearance of Guy Siner ('Allo 'Allo's Lt. Hubert Gruber) as Dr. Mittenhand. While the rest of the cast play the ludicrousness of a leprechaun rampaging through a spaceship offing space marines relatively straight, Davis and Siner don't just chew the scenery; they suck it in like thespian black holes.

As Mittenhand says: "Thank you, Harold, I do the jokes!"

Of course, there is plenty of ropey CGI, as is standard for a 90s genre movie, but there is a wonderful practical creature at the movie's conclusion that pays tribute to David Cronemburg's The Fly. Less Brundle-Fly, more Mitten-Spider. Plus a death that is pure Looney Tunes and a Kaiju-sized leprechaun. Take that, Uber Jason.

4.5 Uber Jasons out of 5. Thank your Lucky Charms

Another horror franchise heading to space for its fourth installment, and this one also came out in 1996. Hellraiser 4: Bloodline marks a real downturn in the fortunes of Hellraiser, being the last in the series to receive a theatrical release and the last to benefit from input from creator and horror maestro Clive Barker.

The film has a portmanteau style beginning in 2127, as Dr. Paul Merchant attempts to solve the mystery of the Lament Configuration, then flashing back to its creation by Merchant's ancestor Phillip LeMarchand in France in 1796. The movie then jumps to 1996, when the Lament Configuration has inspired a skyscraper built by another of Merchant's ancestors.

This second section also sees the franchise's figurehead Pinhead, played by Doug Bradley, come into conflict with the demonic Angelique. A conflict that is carried into 2127.

Arguably, the CGI in Hellraiser: Bloodline is no better or worse than that of Leprechaun 4; the problem is the latter isn't taking itself seriously, but the former really is.

You can't really expect a "fun" Hellraiser movie; that has never been their vibe, and they are better for the serious tone. But it means a poorly realized move to space really doesn't work. Arguably, the biggest crime of Hellraiser 4: Bloodline is that it's a bit dull. The in-depth investigation of the Lament Configuration is only going to appeal to hardcore Hellraiser fans who will probably just end up wishing they'd watched Barker's original 1987 magnum opus movie instead.

And it was all downhill for Hellraiser after this. The franchise became the poster boy for straight-to-video horror, with some later installments developed from scripts that initially had nothing to do with Hellraiser at all. A real insult to a franchise that felt fresh, daring, and even dangerous at its outset.

Pinhead probably wished he'd stayed in space.

2 Uber Jasons out of 5. You'll need your eyes pinned back to finish it

When you have been around since 1897, it is pretty hard to keep your routine fresh. By 2004, Dracula had pretty much exhausted gothic horror; a relocation to a modern setting hadn't saved Christopher Lee's Dracula in the 1970s and had arguably resulted in the worst entries in the Hammer series.

Where else to take the Count in a new millennium but into space? That's the approach taken by Dracula 3000, which doesn't connect to any other Dracula cinema outings but features character names and locales that pay homage to Stoker's original novel. The primary protagonist is Captain Abraham Van Helsing, played by Casper Van Dien, fresh from battling space bugs in Starship Troopers. Dracula — here bizarrely called Count Orlok in an unnecessary nod to Nosferatu — is found on the abandoned ship Demeter by Mother III salvage crew member Mina Harker. Unfortunately, the connections to the source material and the infinitely better Nosferatu are present in name alone. The gothic goodness is gone.

However, something strange happened to me as I was watching Dracula 3000. I found myself enjoying it. Dracula 3000 is... fun?The acting is more wooden than a stake, the dialog is cringy, the characters are so 2D that it is a wonder Drac could draw any blood at all, and the effects are poor. But there is so much here I found myself wanting to show my friends.

Vampire Coolio is a show-stealer; Dracula looks like he has wandered in from a neighboring studio, swanning around a sci-fi setting in full Victorian cape and collar garb. The Demeter hails from the planet Transyvannia, known to be populated by vampires. Drac had no issue procuring oak coffins for his thrall in space. It's all wonderfully silly, and I loved it.

Dracula 3000 isn't as fun as Leprechaun 4, but it definitely isn't boring like Hellraiser 4: Bloodline, and it isn't whatever the heck Amityville is Space is. 3.5 Uber Jasons out of 5. Livin' in a vampire's paradise.

For my money, Leprechaun 4, Dracula 3000, and Jason X would make a cool triple-header of space-horrors for Halloween night. But only 'cause we didn't get the following franchise entry....

OK. Don't Google it. This isn't the Mandela effect at work. The Howling franchise never went to space.

The Howling IV was released in 1988 under the tagline "The Original Nightmare," and though in modern parlance that would indicate a prequel to Joe Dante's 1981 classic, this film is actually a far inferior remake of that first entry in the series.

What a missed opportunity! Though the trope of a fourth film in a franchise going to space, or returning to space in the case of Critters 4, wouldn't be firmly established until 1996, The Howling could have set the ball rolling with its fourth installment.

After all, few horror franchises had suffered the drops in quality seen between the first Howling, a stone-cold classic, and Howling III: The Marsupials (they aren't even werewolves, guys!), with the awful Howling II: Your Sister is a Werewolf between the two.

The Howling was dying like a werewolf with a silver bullet in its guts already by the fourth film; so an early move to space would have been justified. Come on, at least give us werewolves on the moon!

The franchise would limp on for another four films after the Original Nightmare, including a lame duck reboot in 2011, never answering the question: what would happen to a werewolf on the moon? Is the moon always full on the moon, or is it never full because the werewolf can't see it? Fans would forgive this missed opportunity. OK, maybe just me.

1,000 Uber Jasons out of Five. It's werewolves on the moon, people. C'mon!Happy Halloween!

#700. Scarlett Johansson Breaks Silence on ‘The Batman Part II’ Role: “It Was Very Hard to Figure Out”

The actress' character in Matt Reeves' sequel to DC Studios' 2022 film has yet to be revealed.

Scarlett Johansson is opening up about her mysterious role in The Batman Part II, revealing that the part gave her “a lot of existential angst.”

In an interview with Entertainment Tonight, published Wednesday, the actress was asked about her upcoming projects, The Exorcist: Martyrs and The Batman Part II, and which role pushed her furthest out of her comfort zone.

“Probably the role in The Batman,” she responded. “It gave me a lot of existential angst for some reason.”

Johansson went on to explain that the role was particularly difficult to figure out, though she wasn’t sure exactly why. Related Stories Lifestyle Skyler Gisondo on His Style Evolution, Landing His First Fashion Campaign With Bonobos and Playing Ariana Grande's Fiancé in 'Focker-in-Law' TV Earl Barret, 'Too Close for Comfort' Writer and Producer, Dies at 94

“It was very hard to figure out. I don’t know why, whether it was just the role or was just where I’m in my life, or what’s going on, but it was just hard to crack it. And that’s all I can say about it. It was a tough role in a lot of ways,” she added.

Director Matt Reeves confirmed in May that Johansson would be joining the sequel to his 2022 film, which stars Robert Pattinson as Bruce Wayne/Batman. However, details about the character she will portray have yet to be revealed.

In addition to Johansson, new additions to the sequel’s cast include Sebastian Stan, Charles Dance as well as Brian Tyree Henry and Sebastian Koch. (See the full cast here.)

Production on The Batman Part II briefly paused in October after Reeves stepped away to attend to a family matter, according to DC Studios. Liftoff of the NVS-03 mission occurred at 2:21 p.m. ET today (Oct. 30).

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

India bolstered its homegrown satellite-navigation system today (Oct. 30).

A GSLV Mark II rocket launched the nation's NVS-03 satellite from Satish Dhawan Space Centre today at 2:21 p.m. EDT (1821 GMT and 11:51 p.m. India Standard Time).

Everything went well: The rocket deployed NVS-03 into geostationary transfer orbit as planned, officials with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) announced on X about 30 minutes after liftoff.

NVS-03 is the third next-gen satellite that India has launched for the Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC), its version of the United States' Global Positioning System (GPS).

NavIC operates on a smaller scale than its American counterpart, however. It's "a regional navigation satellite system designed to provide accurate Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) service to users in India as well as the region extending about 1,500 km [930 miles] beyond the Indian landmass, which is its primary service area," ISRO officials wrote in the NVS-03 launch brochure.

The Indian constellation currently consists of three fully functioning satellites, and it requires four to provide PNT services. So today's launch was a big deal — and a lot of eyes will be watching NVS-03's commissioning and checkout phase.

Today's launch was the 14th to date for the GSLV (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle) Mark II, a three-stage rocket that stands 170 feet (52 meters) tall. Twelve of those 14 liftoffs have been successful.

The GSLV Mark II debuted in 2010, the same year its predecessor retired. That previous launchers, the Mark I, flew a total of six times, with two failures.

NVS-03 was the fourth Indian launch of 2026 and the third operated by ISRO. The fourth was mounted by Skyroot Aerospace, which in July became the first Indian company ever to successfully reach orbit.

#697. Germany's search for a nuclear waste site

Finland has become the first country with a final storage facility for nuclear waste. Germany is still searching for a site, while some countries have yet to start. Costs are expected to total many billions of euros.

Hardly any environmental and political challenge is as complex as the disposal of radioactive waste from nuclear power plants. In almost all of the world's nuclear-powered nations — some 31 countries currently operate or once operated nuclear power plants — the issue remains largely unresolved. This is despite the first large-scale nuclear power plant going online 72 years ago in the Soviet Union.

Finland recently became the first country in the world to approve a repository for radioactive nuclear waste. Located 400 meters (1,300 feet) underground on an island in western Finland, it is situated at the site of one of the country's two nuclear power plants. The project took around 40 years to complete.

Yet in every other country, including Germany, the problem remains unresolved. To make an everyday analogy: The garbage has already been placed outside for collection, but the garbage truck has not yet arrived. There is simply no landfill to take it to. It is not a pleasant sight, yet hardly anyone wants to live near such a site.

Germany has made some progress: The specially established Federal Company for Radioactive Waste Disposal (BGE) has now been searching for a suitable site for almost ten years, one that, like the Finnish repository, would be located deep underground.

Most experts have long agreed on one point: Nuclear waste, especially the spent fuel elements from nuclear power plants, which will remain radioactive for many thousands of years, must be stored underground.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany hopes to identify a site for a final repository by 2050. But that is still a long way off, which is why Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) wants to examine whether the search process can be accelerated.

And, the government says, at least there is a roadmap in place. "Russia, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Japan have not yet advanced their procedures as far as we have," ministry spokesperson, Stephan Gabriel Haufe, said at a regular government press conference this week. "Finland is certainly the country making the fastest progress worldwide. But Germany is among the leading countries."

This week, the BGE announced that only 5% of Germany's land area, spread across 11 of the country's 16 states, remains under consideration as a potential site for a final repository. The agency is consulting geologists, nuclear experts, and physicists, as well as citizens and politicians. What is already clear, is that the nuclear waste generated during decades of nuclear power production will remain in Germany.

Most of the waste is currently stored at or near the sites where it was generated. These include the 19 former nuclear power plants currently being decommissioned, as well as several research facilities.

In 2011, following the reactor disaster in Fukushima, Japan, Germany decided to phase out the commercial use of nuclear energy, and the last nuclear power plant was shut down in 2023. The waste, however, remains in interim storage.

"It must be shown that a repository will remain safe over a very long period of time," said BGE spokesperson Dagmar Dehmer. "In Finland, that means 100,000 years; in Germany, Switzerland, and France, one million years. But no matter how far into the future scientists project, the effort involved is enormous. It requires a detailed analysis of developments over time, the interactions between geology and technology, and the decay of radionuclides, as well as an assessment of how these factors affect safety."

The procedure is indeed complex: First, potential sites are evaluated for their geological suitability. Will the rock formation remain stable at a depth of 400 meters? Could groundwater become contaminated? The goal is to identify a location where the repository would be surrounded by a rock layer around 100 meters thick, providing a natural barrier. Suitable geological formations include layers of clay, granite, and rock salt.

As the requirements become progressively stricter, fewer and fewer potential sites remain under consideration. Other factors, such as proximity to major cities, come into play only much later in the process. Few communities are likely to welcome a repository for radioactive waste, whether in an urban area or in the countryside.

Building and maintaining trust is also part of Dehmer's job. She often has to explain why it is important to deal with the legacy of the nuclear age, regardless of where people stand on nuclear energy.

Finland has succeeded in doing so, Dehmer believes. "There is a high level of trust in government action in Finland," she said. "The country's supervisory and licensing authority, STUK, is one of its most respected institutions. Germany can learn from Finland by remaining consistent, avoiding frequent changes in direction, and demonstrating the patience needed to achieve a successful outcome."

The disposal of nuclear waste is extremely expensive. Even today, the search for a final repository and the storage of nuclear waste at former reactor sites cost around €1.4 billion ($1.6 billion) per year.

Experts estimate that the final repository itself will cost roughly €14 billion ($16.4 billion) once completed. If all goes according to plan, 28,000 cubic meters of radioactive waste will eventually be stored deep underground on a permanent basis.

This article was originally published in German.
